extracted.intended_audience: political philosophers, constitutional designers, statesmen, and educated readers interested in constitutional theory
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for assessing or designing forms of government (mixed vs simple democracies), focusing on preservation of liberty, restraint of luxury and corruption, separation of powers, protection of minorities, and the capacity to govern large, wealthy polities. Uses historical examples (Athens, Rome, Carthage, Switzerland, Holland) to illustrate institutional strengths and failings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity to preserve liberty in large, wealthy polities
rubrics_metrics.description: A mixed form of government is 'capable of governing a great nation and large territory, whereas the others (simple forms) exist only in small ones; so it is capable of preserving liberty among great degrees of wealth, luxury, dissipation, and even profligacy of manners.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: Simple governments require extreme frugality and simplicity to be tolerable; mixed governments can manage luxury and the moral dangers that come with wealth. Example/implication: Constitutions for populous, wealthy states should favor mixed arrangements rather than pure democracies or pure monarchies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional ability to restrain luxury
rubrics_metrics.description: The danger from luxury lies in excess and human nature; therefore government form should restrain the disposition to luxury by law, education, and discipline rather than assume poverty will secure liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Laws and prohibitions, supported by education and morality, are necessary; mixed governments are best able to implement and enforce such restraints. Anti-pattern: Assuming people will be content with mere 'bread, sports, and ease' and thus not become luxurious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize governors' exposure to baits and snares of luxury
rubrics_metrics.description: 'That form of government... must needs be the most excellent, and the people's liberty most secured, where governors are least exposed to the baits and snares of luxury.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation/critique: The page debates this claim — arguing that simple democracies can actually expose office-seekers to greater temptation because electoral competition forces them to pander with displays and expenditures. Design implication: Constitutions should reduce incentives for officeholders to rely on lavish patronage or personal display to win support (e.g., by checks, stable salaries, limitations on creating offices).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevention of concentration of legislative, executive, and judicial powers
rubrics_metrics.description: A constitution should not vest all authority in one centre (e.g., a single popular assembly) because 'the executive authority must not be prostituted, and the legislative too, to encourage luxury' and because concentration enables corruption, patronage, and partisan justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Separate executive and judicial power from the legislature; provide distinct branches so offices and judgments are not used to reward partisans. Examples: Critique of representative democracies where leaders control purse, create lucrative offices, and capture courts; contrast with mixed systems where ministers are responsible and corruption is subject to inquiry and punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability and enforceability of sumptuary/regulatory laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Sumptuary or anti-luxury laws exist more in popular governments but are usually ineffectual; the ability to execute prudent and reasonable sumptuary laws is a feature of mixed government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Design should ensure laws intended to restrain vice are enforceable; mere enactment without enforcement is ineffective. Anti-pattern: Simple democracies where such laws are 'hated by the people, and violated continually,' and proponents neither dare repeal nor enforce them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for education and discipline by law
rubrics_metrics.description: Disposition to luxury 'can be restrained, where it has the means of gratification, only by education, discipline, or law' and education/discipline lose force when unsupported by law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: Constitutional arrangements should create institutions that combine education, discipline, and enforceable legal norms (a mixed government can sustain these complementary mechanisms). Historical note: rigorous measures alone fail without legal backing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision of fair channels for merit and reward
rubrics_metrics.description: 'A mixed government is the only one where merit can be expected to have fair play: there it has three resources, one in each branch of the legislature, and a fourth in the courts of justice; whereas in all simple governments it has but one.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design guidance: Ensure multiple, independent paths for talent to be recognized (legislative, executive, judicial branches) to prevent arbitrary or partisan distribution of honors and offices. Anti-pattern: Simple governments where rewards depend on will of a single ruler or ruling demagogues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of minority rights and prevention of majoritarian oppression
rubrics_metrics.description: 'There is no freedom nor justice in a simple democracy for any but the majority: the ruling party... will be alive and bold; but the ruled will be discouraged, brow-beaten, and insulted, without a possibility of redress but by civil war.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design implication: Constitutions should include checks and balances and institutions (e.g., an aristocratic senate, separate executive, independent judiciary) that protect minorities from the will of a transient majority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of unchecked assemblies or unlimited power
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Every body of men, every unchecked assembly... had invariably behaved in this manner' (leading to murders, confiscations, tyranny); illimitation of power corrupts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Constitutions should limit duration, scope, and absolute authority of assemblies and officials (term limits, divided authority, review mechanisms). Historical examples: Athens (the Thirty), other unchecked bodies becoming tyrannical; design should prevent such illimitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional resistance to demagoguery and patronage politics
rubrics_metrics.description: When sovereignty (or public purse) is in popular hands, leaders will create offices, commissions, fees, salaries, and perquisites to corrupt voters; they will use judicial and civil law to favor friends and ruin enemies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design guidance: Build institutional constraints on creating patronage, require transparency and accountability for appointments and expenditures, separate purse from short-term electoral manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of parts to cultivate magnanimity and public spirit
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The people under this government are ever endued with a more magnanimous, active, and noble temper of spirit than under the grandeur of any standing power' — but this holds when the people have an essential part, balanced by other branches, not when they exercise the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: Give the populace a meaningful share in sovereignty to encourage civic virtue, but temper that share with checks (senate, distinct executive) to avoid the pathologies of total popular rule. Design trade-off: participation fosters public-spiritedness; unchecked participation risks injustice to minorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of form to territory, population, and commerce
rubrics_metrics.description: Small, poor, or pastoral communities (Swiss cantons, St. Marino) are poor precedents for large, populous, rich states; forms that work in narrow, homogeneous spots may fail in extensive territories with commerce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Choose constitutional form appropriate to scale, population size, wealth, and commercial complexity — mixed governments better for large, wealthy, commercial states like England or American states. Anti-pattern: Transposing institutions from small cantons to large nations without adjustment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical consistency and realistic view of human nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Designers must form institutions adapted to facts about human nature (ambition, appetite for luxury, tendency to imitate splendor) rather than flattering idealized portraits of citizens who will be content with 'bread, sports, and ease.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Constitutional design should assume human tendencies (ambition, corruption, emulation) and incorporate preventive structures (balances, enforceable laws, separated powers). Anti-pattern: Legislators forming institutions based on optimistic, flattering characterizations of the people.
